timeline.title: Evolution of English Tenses & Moods
timeline.description: Milestones in standardizing temporal and hypothetical aspects of English grammar.

cards.details: Old English lacked complex future or perfect tenses, relying on simple past/present forms and prefixes (like *ge-*) to indicate completed action.
Periphrastic auxiliary-driven structures emerged. The verbs 'have' and 'be' were adopted to form present/past perfect and continuous aspects.
Grammarian John Wallis formalized the rules distinguishing *shall* (first person) and *will* (second/third person) in formal English.
Hypothetical clauses (Conditionals 1, 2, and 3) were codified in early pedagogical grammars, emphasizing subjunctive *were* in unreal conditions.
Syntactic structures by Noam Chomsky and others formalized tense as a separate auxiliary component from lexical verbs, dividing time from aspect.

mnemonics.title: Recall Mnemonics
mnemonics.description: Memory hooks to instantly recall tense structures and conditional pairings.

items.title: Mnemonic 1: Since vs. For (Time Reference)
items.decryption:
Rule of time indicators:
• Since is used with a Point of time (e.g., Since 1995, Since Monday).
• For is used with a Duration of time (e.g., For 5 hours, For 2 years).

items.title: Mnemonic 2: Conditional Type 3 Pairings
items.decryption:
The standard structure of the Third (Past Unreal) Conditional:
• If-clause uses had + Past Participle (V3).
• Main clause uses would have + Past Participle (V3).

items.title: Mnemonic 3: Inversion Formula
items.decryption:
To create an inverted conditional, drop the word 'If' and place the auxiliary before the subject:
• *If I had known* -> Had I known
• *If I were a king* -> Were I a king
• *If you should need* -> Should you need

flashcards.title: Active Recall Flashcards
flashcards.description: Hover or click to reveal the answers. Revisit these cards to build instant recall.

items.question: Why is 'If it will rain, we will stay inside' incorrect?
items.answer: Because the conditional (if) clause cannot take future indicators like will or shall. It must use Simple Present: "If it rains, we will stay inside."

items.question: What is the structural rule of the Second Conditional?
items.answer: It expresses unreal/hypothetical present or future states. Structure: If + Simple Past (V2), would + Base Verb (V1). Subjunctive were is used for all subjects.

items.question: When do you use Past Perfect vs. Simple Past for two past actions?
items.answer: Use Past Perfect (had + V3) for the earlier action (first action) and Simple Past (V2) for the later action (second action). E.g., "The train had left before I reached the station."

items.question: Invert this clause: 'If I were to win the lottery...'
items.answer: Drop 'If' and place 'Were' first: "Were I to win the lottery..."

traps.title: Common Exam Traps to Avoid (AHC RO/ARO Focus)
items: Trap 1: Using double future verbs in conditional sentences. In First Conditionals, the conditional clause takes Simple Present, not future. E.g., "If you will work hard, you will pass" is incorrect. Correct: "If you work hard, you will pass".

Trap 2: Incorrectly pairing 'had V3' with 'would V1' in past hypotheticals. E.g., "If she had studied, she would pass the exam." This is incorrect. A past unreal condition requires: "If she had studied, she would have passed the exam."

Trap 3: Misplacing 'since' in present perfect continuous when a duration is given. Remember, since specifies the starting point (e.g., since morning), whereas for specifies the length of time (e.g., for three hours).
Trap 4: Using progressive tenses with stative verbs to show duration. E.g., "I am knowing him for years" is incorrect. You must use Present Perfect: "I have known him for years."

deepDive.title: Tenses & Conditionals Core Study Notes
deepDive.description: Master English tenses, continuous limits, four conditional categories, mixed conditions, and stylistic inversions.

sections.title: 1. Core Tenses & Sequence Rules
sections.content:
A. Present Perfect vs. Simple Past

Tense Time Markers Core Rule & Example
Simple Past (V2) yesterday, ago, in 2012, last week Action finished at a definite past time.
Example: "She left yesterday."
Present Perfect (has/have + V3) already, yet, since, for, recently Action finished in past, linked to present. Do not use past time markers.
Example: "She has left."

B. The Double Past Rule (Past Perfect)

When two actions happened in the past, sequence them as follows:

  • 1st Action (Earlier): Past Perfect (had + V3)
  • 2nd Action (Later): Simple Past (V2)
  • Example: "The train had left (1st) before we reached (2nd) the station."

C. Sequence of Tenses

  • Rule: If Principal Clause is in past, Subordinate Clause must be in past.
    Example: "He said that he was (not 'is') studying."
  • Exception: Keep in Simple Present if expressing a universal truth or fact.
    Example: "He proved that oil floats (not 'floated') on water."

sections.title: 2. Conditionals & Advanced Connectives
sections.content:
A. The 4 Conditional Structures

Type Condition Clause (If) Result Clause (Main) Focus Rule
Zero Simple Present Simple Present Scientific/factual truths.
1st Simple Present will / can / may + V1 Possible future. No future verb in 'if' clause.
2nd Simple Past (were) would / could + V1 Unreal present. Use were for all subjects.
3rd Past Perfect (had + V3) would have + V3 Unreal past hypothetical events.

B. Unless, Until, In Case

  • Unless (if not) & Until (time limit): Do not use *not* or *will/shall* in their clauses.
    Example: "Unless you study (not 'will not study'), you will fail."
  • In Case (precaution): Use present tense instead of future.
    Example: "Take an umbrella in case it rains (not 'will rain')."

C. Mixed Conditionals

  • Past Condition, Present Result: If + Past Perfect, would + V1.
    Example: "If I had won the lottery (past), I would be rich today."
  • Present Condition, Past Result: If + Simple Past, would have + V3.
    Example: "If she were cooperative, she would have helped us yesterday."

sections.title: 3. Inversion, Moods & Stative Shifts
sections.content:
A. Stylistic Inversion (Omitting 'If')

Type Original Structure Inverted Structure
1st Conditional If you should need help... Should you need help...
2nd Conditional If I were a king... Were I a king...
3rd Conditional If they had asked... Had they asked...

B. Imaginary Wishes & overdue Actions

  • It is high time: Followed by subject + Simple Past (V2).
    Example: "It is high time we started (not 'start') studying."
  • Wish / As if: Followed by subjunctive were.
    Example: "I wish I were there." / "He speaks as if he knew everything."

C. Stative vs. Dynamic Shifts

Stative verbs (know, own, belong, taste, have) cannot be continuous. E.g., write "I own a car", not "I am owning".
However, if the meaning shifts to an active dynamic process, continuous is allowed:

Verb Stative (No Continuous) Dynamic (Continuous Allowed)
have I have a house (possession). I am having dinner (eating).
taste The soup tastes good (state). He is tasting the soup (action).
